analysis.one_liner: Requires eye doctors to hand patients their contact lens prescriptions so they can buy lenses elsewhere.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee from April 1995 until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the FTC's eye care rule, patients often had to ask specifically for a copy of their contact lens prescription, and many eye doctors did not volunteer it. That made it hard to buy lenses anywhere but the prescribing doctor's office. This bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to change its rule so eye doctors must offer every patient a copy of the prescription automatically after the fitting is done, or immediately for unchanged renewals. Patients could then comparison-shop for lenses at retail or mail-order sellers.
analysis.who_benefits: Contact lens wearers, who gain the right to a copy of their prescription without asking, letting them buy lenses from cheaper retail or mail-order sellers instead of being tied to their eye doctor's prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires prescribers to offer a copy of the contact lens prescription after the fitting is completed, or immediately for an unchanged renewal, whether or not the patient asks [S3][S2].
With the prescription in hand, a patient can buy lenses from any seller rather than only through the prescribing practice, opening the door to lower prices from retail and mail-order sellers [S3].
Prescriptions would expire after two years unless the prescriber specifies otherwise based on medical judgment, keeping some limit on how long lenses could be reordered [S3].
The bill would not override state laws that release prescriptions on less restrictive terms or state rules on who may fit lenses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Eye care practices, especially optometrists and ophthalmologists, who lose the practical ability to steer patients into buying lenses only from them, giving up the markup on lens sales even though they keep their exam and fitting fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill defines the fitting process as complete only when the prescriber is satisfied a fit has been achieved, which leaves the timing of release in the prescriber's hands and could invite delay [S3].
The two-year default expiration could reduce scheduled follow-up for some patients unless their doctor specifies a shorter interval, a cost an honest supporter should acknowledge [S3].

A good-faith objection: a contact lens prescription is a medical determination, and automatically offering it may push some patients to buy lenses without the professional oversight that ongoing fit and eye-health checks provide [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward and falls on ordinary people: a portable prescription means real price competition on a recurring purchase. The costs fall on eye care practices, which keep their exam and fitting fees but lose lens-sale margins, and the design leaves one escape hatch (prescriber-controlled completion of the fitting) that could blunt the requirement. On balance a modest, consumer-friendly bill whose main flaw is that it could have been stronger.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its trade subcommittee a few weeks later, and no committee ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on April 6, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S5][S1].
On April 27, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials, where it stayed [S5].
The bill attracted 25 cosponsors, 17 Democrats and 8 Republicans, but no further action was ever taken [S4][S5].
The House never voted on the bill, and it died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Eye care practices that profit from selling lenses directly to their own patients are better off, since they kept the ability to withhold prescriptions from patients who never asked. Contact lens wearers, who would have gained the right to shop for lenses elsewhere, are worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Eye doctors who sell lenses directly

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 6, 1995 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill in the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never brought it to a committee vote or the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 25 cosponsors split 17 Democrats and 8 Republicans, so support crossed party lines; there is no record of anyone opposing it on the record, and it stalled in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would force prescribers to hand every patient a copy of the contact lens prescription, ending the practical lock that kept lens purchases inside the prescribing practice. Doctors would keep exam and fitting fees but lose the markup on lens sales, so their interest in the bill ran against patients who wanted cheaper lenses.

industries.industry: Contact lens retail and mail-order sellers
industries.note: With prescriptions portable, sellers outside the doctor's office would gain access to customers who previously had to buy through their prescriber. Their gain comes from lower prices to patients, so their interest runs alongside the public's.
